After two 15-day modifications in late 2017, the driverless testing and deployment rules took effect April 2, 2018.

title: DMV · light-duty delivery vehicle rules
summary: DMV regulations approved December 16, 2019 allow testing and deployment of autonomous light-duty motor trucks, meaning delivery vehicles weighing less than 10,001 pounds, on California public roads. The DMV began approving applications under them on January 16, 2020; heavier vehicles stayed excluded until the 2026 regulations.

title: DMV · draft testing and deployment update
summary: On August 30, 2024 the DMV released draft rules for informal feedback, not a formal proposal, that would remove the ban on autonomous vehicles of 10,001 pounds or more and allow heavy-duty autonomous trucks on roads with posted limits of 50 mph or more and on frontage roads. It drew on 2023 workshops with the CHP and first-responder meetings, and was superseded by the formal April 2025 proposal.

title: DMV · formal regulatory proposal
summary: The DMV's April 25, 2025 formal proposal would repeal the ban on autonomous vehicles of 10,001 pounds or more and create a staged path for driverless heavy-duty truck testing and deployment on specified routes, excluding passenger, oversize, hazardous-materials and bulk-liquid operations. It also added reporting, including vehicle immobilizations, aligned crash reporting with NHTSA, and created enforcement short of permit suspension; comments closed June 9, 2025.

title: DMV · first modified proposal
summary: The DMV's December 3, 2025 modifications, made after comments at the June 2025 hearing, defined an "end user" to separate the owner or lessee from the system manufacturer, aligned emergency-geofencing duties with Vehicle Code section 38751, and defined a "direct route" to keep heavy-duty trucks from detours through residential and school areas. Comments were open until December 18, 2025.

title: DMV · second modified proposal
summary: The DMV's January 21, 2026 second modification revised the definition of "safety case" so manufacturers must describe the standards, methodologies and best practices they applied and how their evidence supports the case, rather than submit all supporting evidence. Comments were accepted through February 5, 2026.

title: DMV · updated testing and deployment rules effective
summary: California's adopted autonomous vehicle regulations (Articles 3.7 and 3.8) took effect April 28, 2026. They open a permit path for autonomous trucks of 10,001 pounds or more hauling property, still excluding passenger-carrying heavy vehicles, oversize loads and bulk-liquid tankers, and require safety cases and reporting of vehicle immobilizations. Peace officers may issue a notice of AV noncompliance, and the DMV may impose restrictions short of suspension.

title: CPUC · passenger service pilots

Drivered pilots keep a safety driver available; driverless pilots must maintain a communication link to remote operators throughout service, and no fares may be charged.

title: CPUC · paid passenger deployment framework
summary: CPUC Decision 20-11-046 (November 20, 2020, as modified by D.21-05-017) authorized Phase I of two deployment programs, one with safety drivers and one driverless, allowing operators to charge fares for autonomous passenger service. Operators need a DMV deployment permit, and driverless applicants must submit Passenger Safety Plans.

title: CPUC · enhanced passenger service reporting
summary: CPUC Decision 24-11-002, voted November 7, 2024, expanded data reporting for autonomous passenger service: trip-level incident reports covering collisions and non-collision events including citations and stoppages, and incident-level data for stoppages of two minutes or more. Pilot participants above 300 passenger trips a quarter file the expanded reports, and collision reports go to the CPUC and NHTSA within one day.
